subject: Operational Procedures
learning_objective: State final reserve fuel for VFR by day
question_text: Under Part-NCO acceptable means of compliance, what final reserve fuel should an aeroplane on a VFR day cross-country flight plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fuel to fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1,500 ft above the destination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fuel to fly for 10 minutes at maximum continuous cruise power

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fuel to fly for 45 minutes at holding speed

choices.label: D
choices.text: No reserve is needed by day

explanation: AMC1 NCO.OP.125(b): final reserve fuel for aeroplanes is 30 minutes at holding speed at 1,500 ft above the destination for VFR by day. It is 10 minutes for local flights within sight of the aerodrome, and 45 minutes for VFR at night and IFR.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 10 minutes applies only when taking off and landing at the same aerodrome and staying within sight of it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 45 minutes applies to VFR at night and to IFR.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A final reserve must always be planned.

learning_objective: State the minimum fuel to commence a flight
question_text: When no destination alternate is required, what is the minimum fuel with which a Part-NCO flight may start?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enough to reach the destination only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enough for the final reserve only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full tanks on every flight

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enough to fly to the intended landing aerodrome plus the final reserve

explanation: NCO.OP.125(c)(1): when no destination alternate is required, the flight may start only with enough fuel to fly to the aerodrome of intended landing, plus the final reserve fuel.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The final reserve must be added.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The trip fuel to the destination must also be carried.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Part-NCO does not require full tanks.

choices.text: Whenever the cabin pressure altitude is above 13,000 ft

question_text: When must a single-engined landplane be equipped with a life-jacket for each person on board?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On every flight, regardless of route

choices.label: B
choices.text: When flying over water beyond gliding distance from land

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only when flying more than 100 NM from land

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only at night

explanation: NCO.IDE.A.175(a)(1): single-engined landplanes need a life-jacket for each person when flying over water beyond gliding distance from land, or when the take-off or approach path is over water such that a ditching is likely in the PIC's opinion.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The requirement depends on the route over water.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The trigger for single-engined landplanes is gliding distance from land.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The requirement is not linked to time of day.

question_text: Under Part-NCO, which document must normally be carried on board as an original rather than a copy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The journey log

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aeronautical charts

choices.label: C
choices.text: The third party liability insurance certificate

choices.label: D
choices.text: The certificate of registration

explanation: NCO.GEN.135(a) lists the documents to be carried as originals or copies unless otherwise specified. incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Charts must be current and suitable, not originals.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This may be carried as an original or a copy.

question_text: In still air, how do wake vortices behind a large aircraft in flight behave?

choices.text: They rise above the aircraft's flight path

choices.label: B
choices.text: They stay at the aircraft's altitude indefinitely

choices.label: C
choices.text: They dissipate immediately behind the aircraft

choices.label: D

question_text: You are landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway. How should you avoid its wake?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stay below its approach path and land before its touchdown point

choices.label: C
choices.text: Land exactly at its touchdown point

choices.label: D

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The vortices end where it touched down; landing beyond is safer.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Landing short places you in the area of its vortices.

question_text: You are taking off behind a larger aircraft that has just departed. How should you avoid its wake?

choices.text: Rotate after its rotation point and stay below its path

choices.text: Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its flight path

subject: Operational Procedures
learning_objective: Identify winds that keep vortices over the runway
question_text: Which surface wind is most likely to keep a wake vortex lingering over the runway touchdown area?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A strong crosswind of 25 kt or more

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calm wind with strong thermal activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: A light crosswind of a few knots

choices.label: D
choices.text: A strong headwind

explanation: A light crosswind of a few knots can roughly balance the outward drift of the upwind vortex, so it stays over the runway. A light tailwind can also move vortices into the touchdown zone.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Turbulent mixing tends to break up vortices.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A strong wind tends to break up vortices.

subject: Operational Procedures
learning_objective: Recognise a decreasing headwind on approach
question_text: On final approach the headwind suddenly decreases. What is the immediate effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The indicated airspeed rises and the aeroplane balloons above the path

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no effect on indicated airspeed

choices.label: C
choices.text: The aeroplane yaws but the airspeed is unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: The indicated airspeed drops and the aeroplane tends to sink below the approach path

explanation: Because of inertia, a sudden loss of headwind reduces the airspeed. Lift drops and the aeroplane sinks below the path. Power is needed to recover.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That happens when the headwind increases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A sudden wind change changes the airspeed until the aeroplane accelerates.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The main effect of a headwind change is on airspeed and flight path.

subject: Operational Procedures
question_text: An aeroplane flies through a microburst on approach. In what order does it typically experience the wind changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increasing headwind, then downdraught, then tailwind

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tailwind, then downdraught, then headwind

choices.label: C
choices.text: Downdraught only, with no horizontal wind change

choices.label: D
choices.text: Updraught, then headwind, then calm

explanation: A microburst is a strong localised downdraught that spreads out near the ground. Flying through it, the aeroplane first meets increasing headwind (performance gain), then the downdraught, then a tailwind (performance loss). That combination is very dangerous at low height.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The outflow is met first as a headwind.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Microburst outflow causes headwind and tailwind changes.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The core of a microburst is a downdraught.

question_text: Using the rule of thumb that aquaplaning speed (kt) is about 9 x the square root of tyre pressure (psi), at what speed might a tyre inflated to 36 psi start to aquaplane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 36 kt

choices.label: B
choices.text: 54 kt

choices.label: C
choices.text: 324 kt

choices.label: D
choices.text: 108 kt

explanation: The square root of 36 is 6. 9 x 6 = 54 kt. Above this speed on standing water, the tyre may lift onto a film of water and lose braking and steering.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That is the pressure value, not a speed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That multiplies by the pressure instead of its square root.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That uses 18 instead of 9 as the multiplier.

question_text: A single-engine aeroplane's engine fails shortly after take-off at low height. What is the generally recommended action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn back immediately to land on the departure runway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise the nose to gain height before choosing a field

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep climbing straight ahead at full throttle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the nose to keep flying speed and land ahead, turning only a small amount to avoid obstacles

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Raising the nose loses airspeed and risks a stall.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The engine has failed; the priority is to keep flying speed.
